display_name: Wind Gap Woodruff Vineyard Pinot Noir, Santa Cruz Mountains
raw_content:
{
  "hook": "Woodruff Vineyard sits at 2,000 feet on fractured shale and sandstone, above the fog line but still kissed by Pacific wind—Wind Gap's 2014 Pinot captures that tension in translucent red fruit and fierce acidity that makes coastal California Pinot feel like Alpine Burgundy.",
  "wine_summary": "Wind Gap's Pax Mahle built his reputation on whole-cluster ferments and zero-new-oak restraint, techniques that let this mountain site's iron-rich shale speak clearly. The 2014 delivers the house style at its most extreme: pale color, 12.8% alcohol, stems that read as pine needle and green tea against wild strawberry. Santa Cruz Mountains' elevation swing (400–3,000 ft) means Woodruff ripens three weeks after valley floor fruit, preserving malic acid that keeps this wine bright at eight years.",
  "terroir_expression": "Shale and sandstone shards force roots to dive 12 feet for water, stressing vines to tiny berries with skin-to-juice ratios that translate into fierce tannin despite the light color. At 2,000 feet the vineyard sits above daily fog but catches cold ocean air streaming through the Pescadero Gap, so nights drop into the 40s even in August—this diurnal swing locks in bright acids and herbal top notes you rarely taste in California Pinot.",
  "vinification_summary": "Mahle ferments 100% whole clusters in open-top wood vats with native yeasts, a technique that extracts bitter tannins from stems early, then softens them into green-tea complexity during the 20-day cuvaison; the wine ages 11 months in neutral 500-liter puncheons so oxygen exchange polishes edges without adding vanilla oak flavor.",
  "food_pairing": "Nashville hot chicken—high acid cuts the cayenne oil while stem bitterness mirrors the spice. Cedar-plank salmon with miso glaze—smoke and umami echo pine-needle notes. Mushroom duxelles tart—earth mirrors earth. For fine dining: roasted squab with black garlic, where the wine's iron-blood note finds its mirror.",
  "comparable_wines": "Ceritas Hellenthal Vineyard Pinot Noir 2014 — same coastal altitude, even leaner frame. Lioco Pinot Noir The Monument 2015 — Anderson Valley shale and similar whole-cluster profile. Hirsch Vineyards San Andreas Fault Pinot Noir 2013 — neighboring ridge, shared marine influence.",
  "style_profile": "Light-bodied dry red with piercing acidity and stem-driven herbal lift",
  "cellar_recommendation": "Drink 2014 now through 2026; keep at 55 °F—its pale color and low alcohol mean it will bronze faster than richer Pinots.",
  "value_assessment": "$45–55 retail buys you Burgundian technique applied to a California mountain site; at that price it undercuts similar-styled single-vineyard Marin and Mendocino Pinots by $15–20. Worth it if you value transparency over opulence.",
  "market_position": "Sommeliers who list Rhys and Arnot-Roberts grab this for by-the-glass programs where guests want coastal California without the sweet-fruit bomb. Retailers stack it beside Lioco and Ceritas for the 'Santa Cruz Mountains' shelf talker that signals cool-climate cred.",
  "insider_take": "Skip this if you need Pinot to taste like cherry cola—Wind Gap's whole-cluster, no-new-oak regimen gives you pine forest and blood orange first, fruit second. That's exactly why the wine outshines its price tag: it reads like-and-now, not manufactured sex appeal.",
  "aging_potential_years": 12,
  "drinking_window_min_years": 8,
  "drinking_window_max_years": 14,
  "sensory": {
    "acidity": 5,
    "tannin": 3,
    "body": 2,
    "sweetness": 1,
    "alcohol": 2,
    "color_intensity": "pale",
    "aroma_intensity": "pronounced",
    "finish_length": "long",
    "complexity": "complex",
    "quality_level": "very_good"
  }
}
